summary: Reviewed the dvpwa aiohttp application end to end: routing, views, DAO/SQL layer, authentication/session utilities, Jinja2 configuration and templates, service setup, config and migration fixtures. The app is intentionally vulnerable and contains a critical unauthenticated SQL injection, stored XSS enabled by globally disabled autoescaping, disabled CSRF protection, weak unsalted MD5 password hashing, and missing authorization on state-changing endpoints. Coverage was the full Python source tree and templates; static JS/CSS assets and font binaries were not analyzed.

findings.title: Unauthenticated SQL injection in Student.create via student name
findings.description: Student.create builds the INSERT statement with Python string interpolation of the attacker-controlled 'name' value instead of a parameterized query. The value flows unfiltered from the POST /students/ handler (views.students, line 57: Student.create(conn, data['name'])), which performs no authentication check, so any anonymous visitor can inject arbitrary SQL. Because the input is wrapped in single quotes, a payload like  x'); DROP TABLE marks;--  or a stacked/UNION query breaks out of the string literal. With PostgreSQL this permits reading the users table (including pwd_hash of superadmin), data destruction, or privilege changes. This is the most severe issue in the codebase. (Other DAO methods correctly parameterize; this is the sole string-formatted sink.)
findings.evidence: q = ("INSERT INTO students (name) " "VALUES ('%(name)s')" % {'name': name})  then cur.execute(q)  — name originates from unauthenticated request.post()['name'] in views.students (line 54-57).
findings.recommendation: Use a parameterized query: cur.execute("INSERT INTO students (name) VALUES (%(name)s)", {'name': name}). Never interpolate user input into SQL text.

findings.title: Stored XSS from globally disabled Jinja2 autoescaping
findings.description: aiohttp_jinja2 is configured with autoescape=False, so no template output is HTML-escaped. User-controlled data persisted to the database is rendered verbatim, producing stored XSS. The clearest sink is course review text (templates/course.jinja2:22 {{ review.review_text }}), created by the unauthenticated POST /courses/{id}/review endpoint (views.review line 129). Other reflected/stored sinks include student.name (templates/students.jinja2:16), course.title/description (templates/course.jinja2:14-15), and login error strings. An attacker submits a review containing <script>...</script> that executes in every visitor's browser; combined with the non-HttpOnly session cookie it enables session hijacking.
findings.evidence: setup_jinja(app, loader=..., context_processors=[...], autoescape=False) — and templates emit {{ review.review_text }}, {{ name }}, {{ course.description }} without |e or escaping.
findings.recommendation: Set autoescape=True (the Jinja2 default) and explicitly mark only trusted content as safe. Remove autoescape=False.

findings.title: CSRF protection middleware disabled on all state-changing POST routes
findings.description: A working csrf_middleware exists (middlewares.py:26-38) and templates embed _csrf_token hidden fields, but the middleware is commented out of the application's middleware list, so no CSRF token is ever validated. Every POST route (login, create student, create course, create review, evaluate/assign marks, logout) is therefore vulnerable to cross-site request forgery. An attacker can host a page that auto-submits a form to /courses/{id}/review or /students/{id}/evaluate/{course_id} against an authenticated victim.
findings.evidence: middlewares=[session_middleware, # csrf_middleware, error_middleware] — csrf_middleware line is commented, and no handler calls token validation.
findings.recommendation: Re-enable csrf_middleware in the middleware chain and ensure all POST handlers receive a valid, session-bound token.

findings.title: Missing authorization on state-changing endpoints (mark evaluation, create student/course/review)
findings.description: The evaluate handler assigns grades (Mark.create) to students and is treated as an admin-only action in the UI (course.jinja2:41 gates the evaluate form behind auth_user.is_admin), but the server performs no authentication or admin check — there is no @authorize(ensure_admin=True) decorator and no user lookup. Any anonymous client can POST to /students/{id}/evaluate/{course_id} and forge marks. The same missing-auth pattern applies to views.students (create student, line 51-60), views.courses (create course, line 83-93) and views.review (create review, line 111-131): all mutate data without requiring a logged-in user. The authorize() decorator exists (utils/auth.py:12) but is only used on logout.
findings.evidence: async def evaluate(request): ... await Mark.create(conn, student_id, course_id, data['points']) — no get_auth_user/authorize call; compare course.jinja2:41 {% if auth_user.is_admin %} which the server never enforces.
findings.recommendation: Apply @authorize(ensure_admin=True) to evaluate and @authorize() (or admin where appropriate) to the create endpoints, enforcing the privilege server-side rather than only in templates.

findings.title: Weak unsalted MD5 password hashing in User.check_password
findings.description: Passwords are hashed with a single unsalted MD5 (check_password compares md5(password) to the stored pwd_hash; fixtures seed users the same way, e.g. md5('superadmin') for the admin). MD5 is fast and broken for password storage: identical passwords yield identical hashes (no salt), and the hashes fall instantly to rainbow tables / GPU cracking. If the users table is read (e.g. via the SQL injection above), every password is trivially recovered, including the admin account.
findings.evidence: return self.pwd_hash == md5(password.encode('utf-8')).hexdigest() ; migrations/001-fixtures.sql:10 VALUES ('Super', NULL, 'Admin', 'superadmin', md5('superadmin'), TRUE).
findings.recommendation: Use a slow, salted password hash (bcrypt, scrypt, or Argon2) and migrate existing hashes; compare with constant-time verification provided by the hashing library.

findings.title: Session cookie set with HttpOnly disabled
findings.description: The RedisStorage session backend is instantiated with httponly=False, so the session cookie is readable by client-side JavaScript. Combined with the stored XSS (autoescape disabled), an injected script can exfiltrate the session cookie via document.cookie and hijack authenticated sessions, including the admin's.
findings.recommendation: Remove httponly=False (default is True) and also set secure=True and an appropriate SameSite attribute for the session cookie.

findings.title: aiohttp application debug mode enabled
findings.description: The Application is constructed with debug=True (and run.py configures DEBUG-level logging). In a deployed instance this enables verbose diagnostics and more detailed error behavior that can leak internal information to attackers. It should not be hardcoded on for production.
findings.recommendation: Drive debug from configuration/environment and default it to False; keep logging at INFO or higher in production.

findings.title: Default/hardcoded database credentials in committed config
findings.description: The database section ships default credentials (user postgres / password postgres****) committed to the repository and used directly to build the DSN in services/db.py. These are development defaults, but hardcoded credentials in source are routinely reused in deployment and should be externalized; if this config reaches a real environment the DB is trivially accessible. Rotate if ever used beyond local development.
findings.evidence: db: user: postgres / password: postgres**** / host: postgres (consumed by services/db.py:15-18 dsn format).
findings.recommendation: Load credentials from environment variables or a secrets manager; keep only placeholders in committed config and rotate any credential that has been used outside local dev.
